claim: RNA-protein interactions (RPIs) are promising targets for developing new molecules of therapeutic interest.
source: RNA-protein interactions (RPIs) are promising targets for developing new molecules of therapeutic interest.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting the premise of the work, supported by the citation to Einstein et al., 2021 in the introduction.

claim: Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1) is a messenger RNA-binding protein involved in cancer progression and resistance to chemotherapy.
source: Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1), a messenger RNA-binding protein involved in cancer progression and resistance to chemotherapy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction (Kang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2010; El-Naggar et al., 2019).

claim: The integrative approach led to the identification of 22 hits validated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
source: This approach led to the identification of 22 hits validated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of which 11 were found to significantly interfere with the binding of messenger RNA (mRNA) to YB-1 in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 2, 4, and throughout the results section.

claim: 11 of the 22 hits were found to significantly interfere with the binding of mRNA to YB-1 in cells.
source: This approach led to the identification of 22 hits validated by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of which 11 were found to significantly interfere with the binding of messenger RNA (mRNA) to YB-1 in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by cellular data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: One of the leads is an FDA-approved poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP-1) inhibitor.
source: One of our leads is an FDA-approved poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP-1) inhibitor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing P1 (Niraparib) as a hit in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: The human genome contains more than 1000 transcripts encoding RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).
source: As revealed by genomic approaches (Van Nostrand et al., 2020; Castello et al., 2012), the human genome contains more than 1000 transcripts encoding RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), thus providing a large variety of interactions with coding or non-coding RNAs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to genomic studies (Van Nostrand et al., 2020; Castello et al., 2012).

claim: YB-1 preferentially binds coding sequences and 3'-UTRs across most transcripts with a weak specificity according to CLIP analysis.
source: However, YB-1 is mostly a core component of untranslated messenger ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) in the cytoplasm (Singh et al., 2015) which, according to crosslinking immunoprecipitation coupled to sequencing (CLIP) analysis (Wu et al., 2015), preferentially binds coding sequences and 3'-UTRs across most transcripts with a weak specificity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to CLIP analysis (Wu et al., 2015).

claim: YBX1 is one of the genes whose gene-protein expression is the most correlated in cancers vs. normal tissues.
source: Interestingly, YBX1 is also one of the genes whose gene-protein expression is the most correlated in cancers vs. normal tissues (Kosti et al., 2016), and YBX1 was identified among the few genes in a clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) screen showing the highest sensitivities with broad proteome co-expression in cancer cell lines (Nusinow et al., 2020, Figure S4 of this reference), pointing toward a possible role for YBX1 in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kosti et al., 2016.

claim: YB-1 is one of the host proteins implicated in viral replication of HIV and SARS-CoV-2.
source: Moreover, YB-1 is one of the host proteins implicated in viral replication of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Jung et al., 2018; Poudyal et al., 2019) and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (Schmidt et al., 2021) and hence targeting it along with targeting specific viral proteins can help reduce viral replication to a higher extent than just targeting the viral proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jung et al., 2018; Poudyal et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2021.

claim: A druggable pocket was found by molecular dynamics simulations located on the outside surface of the CSD β-barrel.
source: Based on our discovery of a druggable pocket by molecular dynamics simulations (MD) located on the outside surface of the CSD β-barrel (which is also part of the RNA binding interface Yang et al., 2019), we implemented a large-scale computational approach that balances accuracy and computational cost to virtually screen potent compounds from small molecule libraries containing more than 7 million molecules.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and described in the results section.

claim: The Quercetin-pocket is located at the third β-hairpin and is monitored by K118 and F85 side chains.
source: Results show that the Quercetin-pocket in its unbound form presents an open and a closed state. This pocket is located at the third β-hairpin and is monitored by K118 and F85 side chains.
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The opening mechanism of the Quercetin-pocket is controlled by an electrostatic cation-π interaction formed between the cationic side chain of K118 (NH3+) and the π-electron ring system of F85.
source: The opening mechanism is controlled by an electrostatic cation-π interaction formed between the cationic side chain of K118 (NH3+) and the π-electron ring system of F85 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Key residues implicated in RNA binding located in the Quercetin-pocket include W65, Y72, F74, F85, H87, K118, and E121.
source: MD and NMR analysis of YB-1 in complex with 5-nt long poly(C) RNA (C5) show that some of the CSD key residues implicated in RNA binding are located in the Quercetin-pocket; these residues include W65, Y72, F74, F85, H87, K118, and E121 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MD and NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The computational approach virtually screened a database composed of 208 million pharmacophores representing around 7.3 million distinct commercially available molecules from MolPort.
source: We started by using a pharmacophore approach to virtually screen a database composed of 208 million pharmacophores representing the conformers of around 7.3 million distinct commercially available molecules from MolPort
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used in the study.

claim: From the 7.3 million MolPort molecules, 78 molecules were finally retained after applying physico-chemical and purchasability filters.
source: From the 7.3 million MolPort molecules, 78 molecules were finally retained.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the computational filtering process.

claim: 62 FDA-approved drugs were selected that may target the Quercetin-pocket using automated blind docking.
source: In parallel, we executed an automated blind docking of 4700 FDA-approved drugs (Drugs-lib library Lagarde et al., 2018) using the MTiOpenScreen web server (Labbé et al., 2015) which lead to the selection of 62 molecules that may target the Quercetin-pocket and may be suitable for a repositioning strategy
evidence: This describes the computational screening of FDA-approved drugs.

claim: The MT bench assay has a SSMD value of 8.1 for a 96-well plate.
source: The measured SSMD value (strictly standardized mean difference) for this assay is 8.1, which is the difference of the mean values of the positive and negative controls divided by the standard deviation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A SSMD value of 8.1 corresponds to an efficient assay.
source: A SSMD value of 8.1 corresponds to an efficient assay whatever the estimated strength of the positive controls (Bray and Carpenter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bray and Carpenter, 2017.

claim: DNA-binding proteins (TOP1, APE1, and LIG1) fail to bring mRNA onto microtubules in the MT bench assay.
source: The results represented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.3 confirm that DNA-binding proteins indeed fail to bring mRNA onto the microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: mRNA enrichment profiles are similar when the same RBP is expressed in cells, regardless of whether classical mRNA IP or microtubule co-sedimentation was used to purify mRNAs.
source: Together the results show a similar profile of mRNA enrichment when the same RBP is expressed in cells, regardless of whether classical mRNA IP or microtubule co-sedimentation was used to purify mRNAs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: 11 of the 22 selected hit compounds significantly decrease the interaction of YB-1 with mRNA in cells.
source: Results show a significant decrease in the slope of the mRNA enrichment on microtubules versus bait expression level for 11 of the tested molecules, all of them were already considered as putative hits in silico, except C6.
evidence: This is supported by MT bench data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The 11 significant hits include 2 flavonols (F2 and F3), 7 chalcones (C1, C2, C3, C6, C8, C11, and C12), a flavonoid analog (A3) and 1 FDA-approved drug (P1).
source: These 11 significant hits include 2 flavonols (F2 and F3), 7 chalcones (C1, C2, C3, C6, C8, C11, and C12), a flavonoid analog (A3) and 1 FDA-approved drug (P1) known as Niraparib, which is a PARP-1 inhibitor notably prescribed for advanced ovarian cancers.
evidence: This is supported by MT bench data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: P1 is Niraparib, a PARP-1 inhibitor prescribed for advanced ovarian cancers.
source: 1 FDA-approved drug (P1) known as Niraparib, which is a PARP-1 inhibitor notably prescribed for advanced ovarian cancers.
evidence: This is a known fact about the FDA-approved drug P1.

claim: Five selected hits (F2, C3, C8, A3, P1) specifically target mRNA interactions with YB-1 and do not significantly affect mRNA:HuR or mRNA:FUS interaction scores.
source: Ten molecules were tested, of which five hits (F2, C3, C8, A3, P1) and five negative controls (P2, F11, F5, D4, C12), and none of them did significantly affect mRNA:HuR or mRNA:FUS interaction scores (Figure 4b). Hence, the five selected hits specifically target mRNA interactions with YB-1.
evidence: This is supported by MT bench data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: 15 of the 25 molecules tested by NMR were confirmed to bind YB-1 in the targeted pocket.
source: In vitro, 15 predicted hits out of 17 were confirmed to bind YB-1 in the targeted pocket by NMR (yielding 88% success rate)
evidence: This is supported by NMR data described in the results section and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The higher selective binding of P1 to the Quercetin-pocket may be due to the interaction of P1 with central (F85, K118, G119) and peripheral (D83, E117) residues.
source: Hence, according to the PCA analysis, the higher selective binding of P1 to the Quercetin-pocket, compared to the other tested ligands, may be due to the interaction of P1 with central (F85, K118, G119) and peripheral (D83, E117) residues.
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 5 and is an inference from the data.

claim: P1 presents a single binding mode to YB-1 as indicated by NMR titration.
source: The superposition of the titration spectra produced a straight line (and not curved plots) which is indicative of a single binding mode (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: STD NMR epitope mapping of P1 confirms the 3D structure of P1 bound to YB-1 obtained by MD simulations.
source: The resulting epitope mapping confirms the 3D structure of P1 bound to YB-1 obtained by MD simulations.
evidence: This is supported by STD NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and MD simulation data.

claim: The highest contributing residues to P1 binding are F85 with –25.5 kJ.mol– 1 and K118 with –19.8 kJ.mol– 1.
source: The highest contributing residues to the binding are F85 with –25.5 kJ.mol– 1 and K118 with –19.8 kJ.mol– 1, where P1 is retained in the Quercetin-pocket by a hydrophobic sandwich (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: YB-1 mutant F85A no longer interacts with P1 according to MD and NMR results.
source: MD and NMR results show that YB-1 mutant F85A no longer interacts with P1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by MD and NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The binding pocket collapses due to F85A mutation.
source: The structural investigation of MD results reveal that the binding pocket collapses due to F85A mutation since F85 maintained the aromatic side chains of residues H87, Y72, F74 and W65 along with K118 in place (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c.

claim: P1 shows weak and nonspecific binding to LIN28(CSD) according to NMR results.
source: NMR results show that some residues in the LIN28(CSD) pocket were experiencing CSPs but to a significantly lesser extent than YB-1(CSD). In addition, we noticed that CSPs in LIN28(CSD) residues are located outside of the Quercetin-pocket, demonstrating a weak and nonspecific binding to LIN28(CSD) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a.

claim: No relevant interaction was detected between P1 and HuR(RMM2) by NMR.
source: Regarding P1 binding to HuR(RMM2), no relevant interaction was detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3b.

claim: P1 can interfere with the binding of YB-1 to mRNAs in vitro as shown by NMR analysis.
source: Results show additional CSPs associated with P1, apart from those due to RNA:YB-1 interactions, which indicates the presence of both YB-1:RNA and YB-1:P1 complexes in solution.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: C8 shows similar competing behavior with RNA for YB-1 binding as P1.
source: Similar competing behavior was also observed for C8, another hit used here as a positive control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 (middle panels) and 7)
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: P2 (Olaparib) showed no effect on RNA:YB-1 interactions in vitro.
source: while P2 (Olaparib, another PARP inhibitor used here as a negative control) showed no effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, lower panels).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant CSPs in YB-1 residues were detected in the presence of P2, P3 or P4 in vitro.
source: and no significant CSPs in YB-1 residues were detected in the presence of P2, P3 or P4 in vitro (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: YB-1 granules formed by P1 treatment are distinct from stress granules triggered by Arsenite.
source: While YB-1 granules can be considered nonspecific stress granules related to cellular stress, they were distinct from stress granules (SGs) triggered by Arsenite (Khong et al., 2017; Bounedjah et al., 2014), a potent and widely used inducer of SGs in cells (large cytoplasmic SG in Figure 8a, upper right panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8a and citations to Khong et al., 2017; Bounedjah et al., 2014.

claim: mRNAs were poorly recruited in YB-1 granules formed by P1 treatment compared to SGs formed in the presence of Arsenite.
source: Consistent with a decreased affinity of YB-1 for mRNAs at high P1 concentrations, mRNAs were poorly recruited in YB-1 granules compared to SGs formed in the presence of Arsenite.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: None of the other PARP-1 inhibitors led to the formation of YB-1-rich granules.
source: None of the other PARP-1 inhibitors led to the formation of YB-1-rich granules (Figure 8a, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8a and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: YB-3 is significantly recruited in YB-1-rich granules formed by P1 treatment.
source: In addition, YB-3, which shares an identical CSD with YB-1, is also significantly recruited in these granules.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1d.

claim: HuR is recruited to a lesser extent than YB-3 in YB-1-rich granules formed by P1 treatment.
source: As a control, HuR which is not a target of P1 is recruited to a lesser extent than YB-3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1d.

claim: In cells treated with two different siRNAs targeting YB-1, P1 did not significantly impair mRNA translation whereas a significant decrease in mRNA translation was measured with the negative control siRNA (siNEG)-treated cells.
source: In cells treated with two different siRNAs targeting YB-1, we observed that P1 did not significantly impair mRNA translation whereas a significant decrease in mRNA translation was measured with the negative control siRNA, (siNEG)-treated cells (Figure 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by puromycin incorporation data shown in Figure 8b and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: P2 had no measurable impact on mRNA translation in both siRNA- and siNEG-treated cells.
source: In contrast, P2 had no measurable impact on mRNA translation in both siRNA- and siNEG-treated cells.
evidence: This is supported by puromycin incorporation data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: All PARP-1 inhibitors decrease the cell number, albeit to a higher extent with P3.
source: Figure 8—figure supplement 5 shows that all PARP-1 inhibitors decrease the cell number, albeit to a higher extent with P3.
evidence: This is supported by cell number data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 5.

claim: Both P2 and P3 further decrease the number of cells in siRNA-treated cells compared to siNEG-treated cells.
source: However, both P2 and P3 further decrease the number of cells in siRNA-treated cells compared to siNEG-treated cells (with significant differences at 5 μM), which may be due to reduced resistance to stress when YB-1 expression is decreased.
evidence: This is supported by cell number data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 5.

claim: P1 rather further decreases the number of cells in siNEG-treated cells when YB-1 levels are high.
source: In contrast, P1 rather further decreases the number of cells in siNEG-treated cells when YB-1 levels are high (non-significant variations but opposite to those observed with P2 and P3).
evidence: This is supported by cell number data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 5.

claim: The separation distance between cells decreases significantly in YB-1-poor cells (siRNA) treated with P1 compared to siNEG-treated cells, in contrast to P2 and P3.
source: The separation distance between cells also decreases significantly in YB-1-poor cells (siRNA) treated with P1 compared to siNEG-treated cells, in contrast to P2 and P3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by cell separation distance data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The appearance of YB-1-rich granules and the inhibition of the YB-1-dependent mRNA translation in HeLa cells are consistent with P1 interfering with mRNA:YB-1 interactions.
source: Therefore, the appearance of YB-1-rich granules and the inhibition of the YB-1-dependent mRNA translation in HeLa cells are consistent with P1 interfering with mRNA:YB-1 interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in Figure 8.

claim: The MT bench assay can fill the gap between in vitro and functional assays by probing whether the interaction of a selected RBP with mRNAs is affected in a cellular context.
source: Here, the MT bench was adapted to score small molecules targeting RBP interactions with endogenous mRNA in cells. The MT bench assays can notably fill the gap between in vitro and functional assays by probing whether the interaction of a selected RBP with mRNAs is affected in a cellular context but not that of other RBPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the MT bench assay based on the results presented.

claim: The computational approach had an 88% success rate in vitro (15 predicted hits out of 17 confirmed to bind YB-1 by NMR).
source: In vitro, 15 predicted hits out of 17 were confirmed to bind YB-1 in the targeted pocket by NMR (yielding 88% success rate)
evidence: This is a summary of the in vitro validation results.

claim: The computational approach had a 50% success rate in cells (11 out of 22 were found to inhibit RNA:YB-1 interactions).
source: and in cells, 11 out of 22 were found to inhibit RNA:YB-1 interactions (50% success rate, while only C6 of the 18 negative controls emerged as a significant hit).
evidence: This is a summary of the cellular validation results.

claim: The molecules selected in this study are multi-aromatic ring systems that are sandwiched in the Quercetin-pocket.
source: All of the molecules selected in this study are multi-aromatic ring systems that are sandwiched in the Quercetin-pocket.
evidence: This is a general observation about the chemical nature of the selected molecules based on structural data.

claim: F85 and K118 are common anchoring key residues for the selected ligands.
source: Besides their common anchoring key residues, F85 and K118, other interactions with neighboring residues, from both sides of the pocket, are needed to stabilize the ligands in the binding pocket, as clearly indicated by the PCA analysis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5 and MD simulation data.

claim: The molecules belong to the flavonoid family with known anti-inflammatory or anti-tumor activity in humans, except for C3, C4, C8-C10, and the A series.
source: Apart from the FDA-approved inhibitors, these molecules belong to the flavonoid family with known anti-inflammatory or anti-tumor activity in humans (Panche et al., 2016), except for C3, C4, C8-C10, and the A series for which no known activity was reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Panche et al., 2016 and knowledge about the molecules.

claim: P1 displays the highest selectivity by targeting key residues from all sides of the pocket via mostly vdW interactions.
source: The top lead, on which we focused the rest of our analysis, is P1, an FDA-approved PARP-1 inhibitor. Based on an exhaustive structural analysis, P1 displays the highest selectivity by targeting key residues from all sides of the pocket via mostly vdW interactions (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis in Figure 5 and MD simulation data in Figure 6.

claim: P1 represents a clear specificity to mRNA:YB-1(CSD) interactions when compared to LIN28(CSD) and HuR(RRM2) in vitro.
source: Moreover, it represents a clear specificity to mRNA:YB-1(CSD) interactions when compared to LIN28(CSD) and HuR(RRM2) in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Functional assays show a global decrease in YB-1-related mRNA translation, cell proliferation, and the appearance of YB-1-rich granules in HeLa cells treated with P1.
source: In addition, functional assays show a global decrease in YB-1-related mRNA translation, cell proliferation, and the appearance of YB-1-rich granules in HeLa cells treated with P1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: The pronounced hematological adverse effects of P1, particularly thrombocytopenia, may be explained by the role YB-1 in megakaryocyte versus erythroid differentiation.
source: For instance, the pronounced hematological adverse effects, particularly thrombocytopenia (LaFargue et al., 2019) may be explained by the role YB-1 in megakaryocyte versus erythroid differentiation (Bhullar and Sollars, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to LaFargue et al., 2019 and Bhullar and Sollars, 2011.
